title: What is known about 1RB1LF_1LC1RB_1LE1LD_1LB0RD_1LF---_1LA0LA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LF_1LC1RB_1LE1LD_1LB0RD_1LF---_1LA0LA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape. Seen in pairs of cells, each visit of the growing left end applies one recursive map to the tape; that map runs a counter in base 4 whose levels are long blocks of the word 111010. The counter itself can never halt; what the head does on the rare occasions it reaches the right end is not understood.
verdict: The question is open. The map from one wall visit to the next is known exactly as a recursion on words of pairs, with exact step counts, and the counter phases are proved in Lean. An accelerated simulator that finds its own rules, checked against direct simulation at every one of 1,399 wall visits (word and step number), runs to wall visit 4.233·102237 (step about 3.1·104475) without a halt. It is exact by construction but has not been re-derived independently. The right-end events do not stop, each one can in principle leave a halting word (such words exist, proved in Lean), and no invariant is known.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 48,278 cells have been visited and 35,368 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Where a halt can come from
claims.text: A closed tape language from windows of 6 cells (closed: yes) covers the run; the only places it lets the halting transition E1 fire are E reading a 1 with the abstract left side in a window of 0s, followed by at least six 1s. With windows of 4 and 8 the same picture.

claims.title: An exact accelerated simulator
claims.text: py/blocksim.py keeps the tape as runs of 111010 and crosses each run with a shift rule; at every visit of the left wall up to 2·106 steps its tape equals the C simulator's (py/bscheck.py).

claims.title: The pair moves
claims.text: With X = 10, Y = 11, O = 00: F moving left swaps X and Y and turns round on a blank pair (reflect, flipX0/1, flipY0/1); Y B> X X becomes <F Y Y Y (turn0/1); Y B> X Yd X becomes X Od-1 Y Y Y B> (digit1, digit). For every count and every surrounding tape.

claims.title: The first-block counter, phase by phase
claims.text: bounce, phase1, phase2, phase4_in, phase4_out: eight wall visits take 000 (1 0)n 0000000 R (digits) to 000 (1 0)n+2 0000000 R', for every n and every tape R, in 104n + 407 steps plus the time spent in R; R' is what one visit makes of R.

claims.title: A word of pairs that halts
claims.text: The wall visit of the tape X Y^8 X X halts after 257 steps. It is not a tape of the run from blank; it shows that the pair structure alone does not exclude a halt.

claims.title: The visit map is a recursion on words
claims.text: V(S) = G(S) with G(Y<sup>a</sup> X X U) = X<sup>a</sup> Y Y Y U, G(Y<sup>a</sup> X Y<sup>k</sup> X U) = X<sup>a</sup> Y G<sup>k</sup>(Y Y U), G(Y<sup>a</sup>) = X<sup>a</sup> Y Y: checked against the machine on 20,000 random words and on every covered wall visit of the run from blank tape (the recursion does not cover the right-end events).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>13</sup> steps
claims.text: A direct simulator on blocks of 16 cells with a full table (c/mrun.c in the folder of 1RB1LE_0LC1RE_---1LD_0RD1LA_0RF1RF_1RA0LB) runs 1013 steps without a halt; the tape then reaches 313,099 blocks, about 5.0 million cells, to the left. The head reaches the right end of the tape at steps 1,937, 4,828, 24,290, 26,031, 17,047,480,846, 19,980,179,600 (tools/c/tmrun.c, to 2·1010) and not again up to 1013.

claims.title: After the reset, a plain counter again
claims.text: After the reset at step 19,980,179,598 the new counter eats the blank stretch and then the frozen first block (turned into blanks from its right end); at 10<sup>11</sup> steps the tape is again a counter with the wall at the left end. At the border of the rest of the tape the head of a carry crosses in the states D, F, B, D, D, F (in, out, in, out, in, out) at all 733 carries of a test, so a level does not depend on what lies to its right. An accelerator that strips levels stalls at stretches between levels that change from hit to hit.

claims.title: The recursion with step counts, checked against the machine
claims.text: On digit words: G(a T) = 0^a h(T) in 16 + 4a steps, h(0 T) = 3 + T, h(k T) = 1 + G^k(2 + T) in 2k steps plus the sub-visits, a unit 1 0 passes a hit in 26 steps. Fitted and then checked on 3,995 random words; the accelerated simulator built on it agrees with direct simulation, word and step number, at 1,399 wall visits (visits 1 to 1,396 (3·10<sup>6</sup> steps) and visits 298,224 to 298,226 (step 100,001,215,143, after the reset)), with jumps of 1, 7, 50 and 1,000 visits.

claims.title: Accelerated run: no halt up to wall visit 4.233·10<sup>2237</sup> (step about 3.1·10<sup>4475</sup>)
claims.text: The digit engine finds cycle, run and recursion rules by symbolic execution and the macro simulator does the right-end events on cells. The run passes the events after wall visits 3, 14, 23, 114, 117, 107,452 and 6.354·10<sup>2236</sup> and stops at the event after 4.233·10<sup>2237</sup>, where a fuel run of more than 10<sup>14</sup> units needed a rule the engine did not have. That rule (frozen words emitted by cycle rules, 16 November 2026) now exists, and the run of 16 November 2026 gets past that point and well into the return sweep of the event, with no halt: after 2 h 35 min, 14,635 runs of cells are left of the head, from 18,141 when the stall point was passed. It is slow there, not stuck. Each wall visit costs about 200,000 explicit operations of the recursion, and rule discovery is not the bottleneck. Exact by construction, validated only on the range direct simulation can reach, not re-derived independently: read it as strong evidence, not as a proof.

claims.title: The counting laws of the level-stripping accelerator
claims.text: first_pass_correct: a level with cycle length p that passes one hit per cycle at position t makes its m-th pass at its hit p(m − 1) + t. blocks_closed: the hits that K super-cycles of an eater need from above, when each block maps x ↦ (c + 1)x + b, are a geometric sum in closed form, for every K. Arithmetic only: the constants come from symbolic runs of the digit engine.

claims.title: From a wall visit straight to the next right-end event
claims.text: The level-stripping accelerator treats the ladder of levels as a mixed-radix counter and jumps an eater's K super-cycles at once (h<sup>P</sup>(E[m] X) = Blk E[m − dm] h<sup>c</sup>(X), derived with the fuel m symbolic). From the word at visit 10<sup>1600</sup> it finds the seventh event at exactly wall visit 6.354265240826449…·10<sup>2236</sup>, all 2,237 digits as the digit engine found them by running every visit: in 128 s with plain batches of hits, in 9 s with 7 nested jumps (eaters ×256, ×16, ×1).

claims.title: Two hits that halt whatever is to their left
claims.text: The hit of a last run of 13 Y's, L Y B> X Y13, halts after 690 steps, and the hit L Y B> X Y8 X X after 254, for every tape L to the left (the head never reads L). So any visit, at any depth of the recursion, that hands on one of these hits stops the machine.

claims.title: What an event does, for every tape to the left
claims.text: For b = 11, 12 and 14 to 20 and every tape L: L x Y B> X Yb comes back over the Y in F, as every regular hit does, leaving a word fixed by b; in the recursion this is one more rule, h(b) = g(b). For b = 0 to 10, every prefix Ya (a ≥ 1) and every tape beyond four blank pairs: the wall visit of the word (a, b) ends 7 cells to the left instead of 2, so the pairs to its right are shifted by one cell.

claims.title: The event rule h(b) = g(b) agrees with the machine
claims.text: 44,000 random words whose events all have a last digit b ≥ 11 (490 of them halt): the recursion G extended by h(b) = g(b) and h(13) = halt predicts every visit exactly (direct simulation). The visit of X Y<sup>b</sup> halts for b ≤ 400 only at b = 13. Events with b ≤ 10 instead end 3.5 pairs further left, with the pairs shifted by one cell, and the word 3 + 0<sup>a</sup> f(b).

claims.title: Every word of at most 18 pairs: 409 halt
claims.text: One wall visit of each of the 524,287 words: 409 halt, every other visit reaches the next wall visit, and every visit without an event gives G(S). Whether a word halts depends only on its hit (the word after the first digit): 218 halting hits, roughly doubling with each extra pair. At every event the innermost sub-visit is a two-digit word (a, b); halting is not decided by (a, b) and the frames' counters alone.

claims.title: The run's events meet no halting hit
claims.text: The accelerated run, logged at every visit that ends in an event through all eight right-end events and into the eighth's return: the innermost words are (3, 2), (2, 2), (6, 8), (5, 5), (9, 2), (6, 2), (5, 11) and (2, 8). No last digit is 13, and none of the 26 short hit words of the innermost frames halts when run directly; those of the seventh event (b = 11) return as ordinary hits.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The counter cannot halt. A halt needs a last digit 13 or a halting hit, and the halting hits other than 13 all go through an event with b ≤ 10; no such hit has appeared in the run so far.

claims.title: The right-end events
claims.text: A right-end event is a hit that reaches the last digit b of the word; at its bottom is always a sub-visit of a two-digit word (a, b). For b ≥ 11 it is now understood (an ordinary hit h(b) = g(b), or a halt at b = 13). Events with b ≤ 10 shift the pairs by one cell, and what that does where the shifted visits meet the unshifted pairs of an enclosing frame is not known as a rule: those events are still simulated on cells, and every one is a new chance for a halting hit.

claims.title: No halt in the first 6.60×10<sup>17</sup> steps (exact macro run)
claims.text: A macro simulator (blocks of 6 cells, long runs of equal blocks crossed in one go; exact: every macro step is a run of the machine, counted step for step) ran from blank tape to step 660,252,048,354,256,421 without a halt. At this block size it gives the same state, head position and tape as the direct simulator after 2,000,019,329 steps. This is a bounded run and says nothing about later steps.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts. Cut the tape into pairs of cells: every visit of the growing left end applies one recursive map to the tape, which builds a ladder of counters in base 4 and feeds it with fuel. A program that jumps over the regular parts has followed the machine to step 3.1·10<sup>4475</sup> without a halt; the rare moments when the head reaches the other end of the tape keep coming and are not understood, and they decide the question.

facts.text: Pair moves and the four phases of the counter, proved in Lean for every tape.
A word of pairs on which a visit halts: the structure alone does not decide.
Steps without a halt in the accelerated run (validated on the part direct simulation can reach).
An event with last digit 13 halts for every tape to its left; those with 11, 12, 14 to 20 are ordinary hits.

sections.heading: Pairs of cells: X = 10, Y = 11
html: Each time the head is in state F on a 0 with only 0s to its left (a wall visit) the tape to its right is a word of the pairs X = 10 and Y = 11. The wall is the growing end: it moves one pair to the left at every visit. The right end of the tape stays where it is for very long stretches.
From one wall visit to the next the word S becomes G(S):

G(Y^a X X U)     = X^a Y Y Y U                 turn back at the first double X
G(Y^a X Y^k X U) = X^a Y G^k(Y Y U)            a digit k: k visits of the rest
G(Y^a)           = X^a Y Y                     the blank right end, reached in B

What the head does: B runs right over the Y's. At a double X it turns back. At X Y^k X it erases the k Y's and refills two pairs, so k − 1 blank pairs stay behind it. On the way home F swaps X and Y in every pair, and a blank pair sends it right again: each blank pair is a small wall for the rest of the tape. These moves are proved in Lean (turn, digit, flip, reflect).

sections.heading: A counter in base 4, level after level
html: Write the word as digits (the number of Y's before each X). The six-cell word 111010 is the digit pair 1 0, and the tape is 000 (1 0)N1 w ... (1 0)N2 w ... (1 0)N3 w .... The digit word w behind a block goes through four phases:

One phase is two wall visits. The block gains one 1 0 in the second and in the fourth phase, and in the fourth the head goes on into the rest of the tape. For the first block all of this is a Lean theorem for every block length n and every tape R behind it: eight visits take 000 (1 0)n 0000000 R to 000 (1 0)n+2 0000000 R', and R' is exactly what one visit makes of R. So the rest of the tape lives the same life, eight visits to one: the second block grows four times more slowly than the first, the third sixteen times, and so on (5998, 1492, 372, 88, 21 copies after 109 steps).

sections.heading: When the head reaches the right end
html: When the last level overflows the head arrives at the blank right end in state D, and the recursion no longer applies. In the first 2·1010 steps this happened at steps 1,937, 4,828, 24,290, 26,031, 17,047,480,846, 19,980,179,600. Some of these events only rewrite the last few digits; others are resets: a stretch of blank pairs is left inside the tape, a new counter starts to its right and uses the stretch as its wall, and the old blocks stay frozen until the stretch is used up.

The machine stops only when E reads a 1. The counter never brings that about, but some words of pairs do: on the tape X Y^8 X X a single wall visit halts after 257 steps (a Lean theorem; this tape does not occur in the run from blank). So whether the machine halts depends on the words that the right-end events leave behind. The next section takes an event apart.

sections.heading: Inside a right-end event
html:
A right-end event is a hit that reaches the last digit b of the word. The visit that does it always comes down, at the bottom of the recursion, to a two-digit word (a, b): every level of the recursion shortens the word by one digit, so the last sub-visit before the end sees just two. On cells the head then erases the last b Y's (state D) and runs into blank tape. The b erased pairs become b small walls, and a fresh counter starts on them from the word 2, one pair per visit, shifted one cell against the pairs to its left. What happens next depends on b:

last digit bwhat the event does (with enough blank pairs to its left)evidence
0 to 10The visit ends 3.5 pairs further left than usual, in the other pair alignment, with the word 3 + 0a f(b). The visits after it are the same recursion G, shifted by one cell; the shift only matters where it meets the unshifted pairs of an enclosing frame.Lean for every a ≥ 1 and every tape beyond four blank pairs (shift0 to shift10)
13The machine halts, whatever is to the left: the counter on the 13 erased pairs runs into the Y in front of them and E reads a 1 (690 steps).Lean, every left tape (hit13_halts)
11, 12, 14 and upAn ordinary hit: the head comes back in F as after any hit, and the event is one more rule of the recursion, h(b) = g(b) for a fixed word g(b).Lean for b = 11, 12, 14 to 20, every left tape; 44,000 random words with such events agree with the machine

The words for an event right at the wall (a = 0):

b =  0..10 (shifted):  5 | 3 0 2 | 8 | 3 0 0 0 0 2 | 6 0 0 2 | 3 0 0 3 2 | 6 3 2 | 3 0 0 1 0 0 5 | 6 1 0 0 5 | 3 0 0 1 0 8 | 6 1 0 8
g(11) = 0 0 0 3 3 1 0 0 5     g(12) = 0 6 3 1 0 0 5     g(13): halt     g(14) = 4 0 3 3 1 0 0 5
g(15) = 1 0 0 6 3 1 0 0 5     g(16) = 4 6 3 1 0 0 5     g(17) = 1 0 0 4 1 0 0 0 0 0 3 3 1 0 0 5

Which words halt. All 524,287 words of at most 18 pairs were run, one wall visit each. 409 of them halt and every other visit reaches the next wall visit. Whether a word halts depends only on its hit, the part after the first digit: Ya X T halts for every a or for none. There are 218 halting hits of this size, and their number keeps growing with the length, so they are not a short list. The two simplest, 13 and 8 0 0, are Lean theorems for every tape to their left. Most others are a digit 8 or 6 whose first sub-visits end in an event right next to the blank pairs the digit left behind.

The run's events tested. The accelerated run was instrumented at every visit that ends in an event, through all eight right-end events and into the return of the eighth. The innermost words were (3, 2), (2, 2), (6, 8), (5, 5), (9, 2), (6, 2), then (5, 11) many times in the seventh event's return and (2, 8) in the eighth's. No last digit is 13. The hits of the innermost frames (for example 3 3 11, 4 1 0 0 3 11, 9 9 4 1 0 0 3 11) were run directly: none halts, and the ones with b = 11 return as ordinary hits. Halting is not decided by the innermost word and the frames' counters alone: in the 18-pair data the same (a, b) and the same remaining sub-visits of the four innermost frames occur in halting and non-halting words. So the test has to look at the words themselves, which is what the next step needs.

sections.heading: Levels, fuel, an eater, and the rare events
html: Read the word right of the wall as digits: the lengths of the runs of Y between the X's. One wall visit then does this: G(a T) = 0^a h(T), where the hit h is h(0 T) = 3 + T (add 3 to the first digit) and h(k T) = 1 + G^k(2 + T) (the rest of the tape gets k visits of its own). Everything the machine does between two right-end events follows from these three lines, and the number of steps does too.
Four kinds of structure grow out of it:

• a level, (1 0)^n with a small digit word behind it that cycles through four shapes; four hits add two units and pass one hit on, so each level is four times slower than the one before;
  • fuel, a run (1 0 0)^m, made when an old level is taken apart;
  • an eater at the bottom of the ladder of levels, which burns three units of fuel every eleven hits and leaves new small levels behind;
  • a right-end event, when a hit gets through everything and reaches the last digit. Then the head runs to the blank end of the tape and comes back in a different way; some events crush every level into a single digit (a reset), others only turn the newest levels back into fuel.

A program that works on the digits, finds the repeating patterns by itself and jumps over them (it keeps the counts as big numbers) was checked against a plain simulation of the machine at 1,399 wall visits: the same tape and the same step number every time. It then runs on: past the reset, through 102236 quiet wall visits in which the ladder grows to 3,713 levels, through one more event, and up to the event after wall visit 4.233·102237, at step 3.1·104475. No halt. There it meets a run of fuel too long for the patterns it knows, and stops.

The ladder can also be treated as arithmetic: each level is a counter digit with a known cycle, and an eater that burns its fuel a few units at a time builds the same block of levels again and again, so K of its rounds can be jumped at once with a geometric sum (proved in Lean for every K). With that, the program goes from wall visit 101600 straight to the seventh event, at exactly the visit found before by running every visit, in 9 seconds instead of hours.

Why this does not settle the question: the events never stop coming, each one rewrites the far end of the tape in a way that is only known by running it, and there are words on which the machine halts. Nothing so far says that such a word can never be left behind.

explainer.title: One map on words, and a counter in base 4 inside it

family: nested base-4 counter on pairs (word recursion) with fuel, eater and right-end events
summary: Wall visits iterate a recursion on digit words (levels (10)^n in base 4, fuel (100)^m, an eater that builds new levels); an accelerator validated on 10^11 steps follows it through the reset and one more right-end event to wall visit 4.2·10^2237 (step 3.1·10^4475) without a halt, then stalls; events keep coming, so the question is open.
